summary: Analysis of test_capture.pcap identified 10 finding(s) across 1 IPsec session(s) (4 High, 5 Medium, 1 Low). The most significant issue is: Weak encryption algorithm negotiated: 3DES. The combination of weaknesses places this deployment at an overall risk score of 78.2/100 (Critical). Remediation should begin with the highest-severity cryptographic parameters before addressing policy and hygiene items.

findings.evidence: IKE transform payload advertised ENCR_3DES for session 192.168.10.1 -> 203.0.113.50
findings.explanation: The tunnel negotiated a symmetric cipher that no longer provides the effective key strength modern guidance requires. An attacker who can capture the encrypted flow can retain it and attempt offline recovery of the plaintext as compute becomes cheaper.
findings.recommendation: Renegotiate the IPsec proposal to AES-256-GCM (AEAD). If the peer cannot do GCM, use AES-256-CBC with a separate SHA-256 integrity algorithm, and remove DES/3DES from the allowed transform set entirely.

findings.evidence: IKE transform payload advertised AUTH_HMAC_MD5 for session S1
findings.explanation: The integrity/PRF algorithm in use has known collision weaknesses. A weak integrity algorithm undermines the authenticity guarantee of the tunnel: packet tampering becomes cheaper to hide than the cipher strength alone would suggest.
findings.recommendation: Move the integrity algorithm to SHA-256 or above (SHA-384/SHA-512). Delete MD5 and SHA-1 transforms from both the IKE and ESP proposals.

findings.issue: Weak Diffie-Hellman group negotiated: group 2 (1024-bit MODP)
findings.evidence: IKE key exchange payload indicated DH group 2 for session S1
findings.explanation: The Diffie-Hellman group used to derive keying material is too small. Small MODP groups are within reach of well-resourced precomputation attacks, which would expose every session keyed from that group.
findings.recommendation: Use DH group 14 (2048-bit MODP) as a minimum; prefer group 19/20 (ECP-256/384) or group 21. Remove groups 1, 2 and 5 from the policy.

findings.evidence: ISAKMP header exchange type 4 (Aggressive) observed on UDP/500
findings.explanation: The tunnel uses IKEv1, which is deprecated. IKEv1 lacks the built-in DoS protection, reliable rekeying and MOBIKE support of IKEv2, and its aggressive mode transmits identity material before encryption starts.
findings.recommendation: Migrate the tunnel to IKEv2. If IKEv1 must remain during transition, disable aggressive mode and permit main mode only.

findings.evidence: IKE transform payload advertised auth method 1 (Pre-Shared Key)
findings.explanation: Peer authentication relies on a pre-shared key. PSKs are commonly shared across devices, rarely rotated, and — in IKEv1 aggressive mode — can be captured in a form that permits offline cracking.
findings.recommendation: Migrate to certificate-based authentication (RSA/ECDSA) with a managed PKI. Where a PSK must remain, make it at least 32 random characters, unique per peer, and rotate it on a defined schedule.

findings.evidence: No KE payload observed in quick mode exchange for session S1
findings.explanation: Perfect Forward Secrecy is disabled, so child SA keys are derived from the IKE SA keying material. Compromise of that long-term material therefore retroactively exposes traffic from every prior session.
findings.recommendation: Enable PFS on the child SA and pin it to DH group 14 or higher so each rekey performs a fresh Diffie-Hellman exchange.

findings.evidence: ESP sequence numbers did not increase monotonically across 40 packets
findings.explanation: Anti-replay is not in effect for this SA. Without a replay window an attacker who can capture ESP packets can retransmit them, and the receiver will accept and process the duplicates.
findings.recommendation: Enable anti-replay on the SA and set the replay window to at least 1024 packets (larger for high-throughput or multi-queue links).

findings.evidence: ID payload present in unencrypted aggressive mode message 1
findings.explanation: Endpoint identity material is observable in the negotiation. This lets a passive observer map which peers talk to which gateways, and gives an attacker the identity values needed to target credential attacks.
findings.recommendation: Use IKEv2 (which encrypts identity payloads) or IKEv1 main mode, and avoid FQDN/user-FQDN identities that disclose organisational detail.

findings.evidence: IKE SA lifetime attribute decoded as 172800 seconds (> 86400)
findings.explanation: The SA lifetime is outside the recommended window. Very long lifetimes increase the volume of data protected by a single key; very short ones cause constant rekeying that can destabilise the tunnel and burn CPU.
findings.recommendation: Set the IKE SA lifetime to roughly 24 hours and the IPsec (child) SA lifetime to 1-8 hours, with a data-volume based rekey limit as well.

findings.issue: Negotiated cipher suite is not in the approved list
findings.evidence: Suite 3DES/MD5/DH2 does not meet the AES-GCM or AES-256 + SHA256 baseline
findings.explanation: The negotiated cipher suite falls outside the approved baseline (AES-GCM / AES-256 with SHA-256 or stronger). Even where no single parameter is critical, the combination will not pass an audit against current hardening guidance.
findings.recommendation: Align the proposal with the approved baseline: AES-256-GCM, SHA-256+, DH group 14/19+, IKEv2, PFS enabled, certificate authentication.

Endpoint pair and tunnel timing are visible to any on-path observer

detection_notes: Alert on IKEv1 aggressive mode exchanges (UDP/500) originating from any gateway.
Flag ESP SAs whose sequence numbers reset or regress, which indicates replay exposure.
Baseline per-tunnel packet-size distributions; a shift can reveal an application change behind the tunnel.
Track IKE proposals offering DES/3DES/MD5/DH1/DH2 and treat any acceptance as a policy violation.
limitations: Parameters that never appear on the wire (for example a locally configured SA lifetime that is not negotiated) are reported as Unknown.
Encapsulation mode and anti-replay status are inferred from ESP structure and sequence behaviour, not read from configuration.
Traffic classification is probabilistic and based only on size/timing metadata.
